q: Which of these is a subsequence of 'LONGEST' but not a substring?
explain: O, N and E appear in order but not next to each other (G sits between N and E). The other three are contiguous runs, so they are substrings.

q: What is the LCS recurrence when X[i] = Y[j]?
explain: A matching last character can always be added to an LCS of the two shorter prefixes.

q: What is the LCS recurrence when X[i] ≠ Y[j]?
explain: At least one of the two last characters is not in the LCS, so drop one of them and keep the better result. Resetting to 0 would be the longest common substring.

q: What is the LCS length of 'STONE' and 'LONGEST'?
explain: 'ONE' is common to both. No common subsequence of length 4 exists, as the full table confirms with L[5][7] = 3.

q: What are the time and space of the standard LCS DP for strings of lengths m and n?
explain: There are (m + 1)(n + 1) cells, each filled in O(1). Keeping only two rows reduces the space to Θ(min(m, n)) if only the length is needed.

q: Two strings always have exactly one longest common subsequence.
explain: False. For example, 'AB' and 'BA' have two LCSs of length 1: 'A' and 'B'. The trace-back finds one of them.

q: During the trace-back, what do you do when X[i] = Y[j]?
options: Take the character and move diagonally to (i−1, j−1)
explain: Matching cells are where LCS characters come from. On a mismatch, move towards the neighbour with the larger value.

q: What is the LCS of 'AGGTAB' and 'GXTXAYB'?
explain: G, T, A and B appear in order in both strings. A length-5 common subsequence does not exist.

q: How can you find the longest palindromic subsequence of a string s?
explain: A palindrome reads the same in both directions, so it is common to s and its reverse. For 'CHARACTER' this gives 'CARAC' (length 5).

q: In terms of the LCS, what is the length of the shortest common supersequence of x and y?
explain: Write both strings out, sharing the LCS characters only once.
